title: George MacDonald
hook: a Scottish storyteller of God's relentless, fatherly love

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chesterton's fairyland: the plain world, as strange and chosen as any story. Your line was the world is strange.

A young princess climbs a stair in her own castle she's never noticed before, and at the top finds an old, beautiful woman, spinning. The woman says she's the princess's great-great-grandmother. Her nurse doesn't believe a word of it. Later, the grandmother gives the girl a thread so fine she can hardly see it, and tells her to follow it whenever she's afraid. Deep in the dark, under the mountain, the thread leads exactly where she needs to go. That's The Princess and the Goblin, by George MacDonald, a Scottish minister who became a storyteller.

For MacDonald, God's love was like that thread: hard to see, and impossible to break. He called God Father, and meant it at full strength. A good father doesn't stop loving a child who runs off. He keeps going after them. MacDonald heard that in Jesus's story of the son who wastes everything and turns for home, where the father sees him "when he was yet a great way off," and runs. In his Unspoken Sermons, MacDonald takes on a line from Hebrews that can sound frightening: "For our God is a consuming fire." Some readers hear a threat. MacDonald heard love. The fire, he said, burns against everything in us that isn't love, our selfishness, our lies, our hardness, and it won't stop burning until those are gone. But it never burns against us. It's the fire of a love that refuses to give up on what it loves: relentless, which here means tireless, not harsh. Some Christians found MacDonald too hopeful. He was willing to hope that this love might reach everyone in the end, and others pushed back on that, and still do. His admirers say he made God's fatherhood feel like coming home. Either way, he told it through fairy tales: goblins and mountains, a North Wind, a princess with a thread. He seems to have trusted that a child, or a grown-up who'd forgotten how to be one, might understand love through a story before following an argument.

segments.voice: Bring back a story you loved as a child, one somebody read to you at night, and find the moment when someone was lost or in danger and help came. Who came, and what did it feel like back then to hear that part? Sit with that scene for a while, and if you pray, give thanks for whoever first read to you.
George MacDonald. The Scottish minister and storyteller who pictured God's love as a father's fire that never lets go.
Your line: love will not let go. Like a thread too fine to see, and too strong to break. Go gently.

howItsDone: Christians who read George MacDonald often read his fairy tales and his Unspoken Sermons side by side, and some families read his children's books aloud together.
